questions.question: Liam's backyard garden is a rectangle. It is 8 m long and 5 m wide. He wants to put a fence all the way around the outside edge of the garden. How many metres of fence does he need?
questions.explain: A fence goes around the edge, so this is perimeter: add all four sides, 8 + 5 + 8 + 5 = 26 m. The common trap is multiplying 8 x 5 = 40, but that gives the area (the space inside), not the fence.

questions.question: A rectangular patio at a Kelowna school is 6 m long and 4 m wide. It will be covered completely with square tiles that each measure 1 m by 1 m, with no gaps. How many tiles are needed?
questions.explain: Covering a surface means area: 6 x 4 = 24 square metres, so 24 tiles of 1 m² each. The trap is adding the sides (6 + 4 + 6 + 4 = 20), which is the distance around the patio, not the space inside it.

questions.question: Maya's sandbox is a square. Each side is 7 m long. She wants to glue a strip of soft rubber edging along all four sides, right at the outside edge. How many metres of edging does she need?
questions.explain: Edging along the sides is perimeter: 7 + 7 + 7 + 7 = 28 m, or 4 x 7. Watch out for 7 x 7 = 49 — that is the area of the sand inside, not the length around the edge.

questions.question: A rectangular wooden deck behind a house in Nanaimo is 9 m long and 3 m wide. The whole top surface of the deck will be painted. How many square metres of deck get painted?
questions.explain: Painting a flat surface means area: 9 x 3 = 27 m². The usual mistake is adding the sides (9 + 3 + 9 + 3 = 24), which tells you how far it is around the deck, not how much surface there is to paint.

questions.question: A rectangular vegetable plot has a perimeter of 30 m. Its length is 10 m. What is its width?
questions.explain: Half the perimeter is one length plus one width: 30 / 2 = 15, then 15 - 10 = 5 m. A common error is dividing 30 by 10 to get 3, which would only make sense if 30 were an area in square metres.

questions.question: Priya is fencing a rectangular dog run that is 12 m long and 5 m wide. Fencing costs $4 for each metre. How much will the fencing cost?
questions.explain: Fencing is sold by the metre, so first find the perimeter: 2 x (12 + 5) = 34 m, then 34 x $4 = $136. The trap is using 12 x 5 = 60 square metres and paying $240 — that is the ground inside, not the fence line.

questions.question: A square garden bed has an area of 36 m². What is the perimeter of the garden bed?
questions.explain: Work backwards: a square with area 36 m² has sides of 6 m because 6 x 6 = 36, so the perimeter is 4 x 6 = 24 m. The trap is answering 36 m — that number is the area, and area and perimeter are never the same measurement.

questions.question: Noah is putting wooden edging around the outside of a rectangular strawberry patch that measures 7 m by 4 m. Which calculation tells him how many metres of edging to buy?
questions.explain: Edging goes around the outside, so use perimeter: 2 x (7 + 4) = 22 m. Multiplying 7 x 4 gives 28 square metres of soil inside the patch, which is area and would not tell Noah how much edging to buy.

questions.question: A rectangular lawn beside a community centre is 10 m long and 6 m wide. New sod for the whole lawn costs $8 for each square metre, and a fence around the outside edge costs $5 for each metre. What is the total cost of the sod and the fence together?
questions.explain: Do two separate steps: sod uses area, 10 x 6 = 60 m² at $8 = $480; fence uses perimeter, 2 x (10 + 6) = 32 m at $5 = $160; together $640. The big trap is using the area 60 for the fence too, because fencing is measured in metres around the edge, not in square metres.

questions.question: Mateo says, 'My rectangular garden is 10 m long and 4 m wide, so I need 40 m of fencing to go around it.' Which statement is correct?
options: He found the perimeter instead of the area, so he really needs 40 m² of fencing.
He found the area instead of the perimeter, so he really needs 28 m of fencing.
He should use 10 + 4 = 14 m of fencing.
He is right, because 10 x 4 = 40 m of fencing.
questions.explain: Fencing follows the edge, so use perimeter: 10 + 4 + 10 + 4 = 28 m. Mateo multiplied 10 x 4 = 40, which is the area of soil inside the garden in square metres — a length of fence can never be measured in square metres.

questions.question: Ana is covering a rectangular deck that is 8 m long and 5 m wide with square tiles that each measure 1 m by 1 m. She already has 36 tiles at home. Which statement is true?
options: Yes, she only needs 26 tiles, so 10 are left over.
No, she needs 80 tiles, so she must buy 44 more.
No, she needs 40 tiles, so she must buy 4 more.
questions.explain: Tiles cover a surface, so find the area: 8 x 5 = 40 tiles, and 40 - 36 = 4 more to buy. The trap is calculating 2 x (8 + 5) = 26, which is the distance around the deck, not the number of tiles that fit inside it.

questions.question: A rectangular flower bed in a Vancouver park is 7 m long and 4 m wide. Jonah jogs all the way around the outside edge of the flower bed 3 times. How far does he jog in total?
questions.explain: One trip around is the perimeter, 2 x (7 + 4) = 22 m, and three trips are 22 x 3 = 66 m. The trap is using 7 x 4 = 28 m² and tripling it to 84 — that is the area of the flower bed, not the path Jonah runs along the edge.
